structure.title: I. Setting, Experimental Design, Data, and Estimation
II. Delivery of Assistance, Targeting, and Poverty Impacts
IV. Leakage and Administrative Program Costs

observations.statement: The paper states its estimand as the intent-to-treat effect of district-level randomized assignment to the voucher conversion in 2018 versus continued in-kind delivery, estimated by a single cross-sectional regression at endline.

Identification rests on government-run random assignment of districts to the 2018 versus 2019 conversion wave; the paper names this explicitly as a randomized policy experiment rather than a quasi-experimental design.
observations.locator: Section I.C Randomization Process and Compliance

observations.statement: The authors flag that a budget-exhaustion rule made treatment probability non-constant within a reserved 'holdout' stratum of small districts, and state that strata fixed effects are included in every regression to address this.
observations.locator: Section I.C Randomization Process and Compliance

observations.statement: Because only a small number of control districts were converted early, the paper states it studies the intent-to-treat effect rather than a treatment-on-treated estimate, and notes the two would be very similar given the low crossover rate.
observations.locator: Section I.C Randomization Process and Compliance

observations.statement: Two primary data sources are named and linked at the household level via national ID: a purpose-written module added to the national household survey (two waves, baseline and endline) and an administrative targeting database, with a village census also merged in.

The unit of observation is the household within a repeated cross-sectional survey; because no household panel exists, district by urban/rural averages from the baseline wave are constructed and merged in as potential controls.

The 105-district sample is explained as arising from the government's own readiness ranking combined with a binding annual conversion budget, not from a researcher-imposed exclusion rule, and is described as the reason random assignment was possible at all.

Every regression table reports the observation count for each column, with sample size varying systematically across columns as the sample is progressively restricted to narrower baseline poverty-score bands.

The targeting database used for baseline poverty scores is administrative government data linked by national ID and analyzed only in de-identified form, distinguishing it from the publicly documented survey instrument.

The treatment variable is defined as random assignment to the 2018 voucher conversion wave (an intent-to-treat indicator), not actual receipt of the voucher, consistent with the paper's stated intent-to-treat framing.

The main subsidy outcome is constructed by valuing in-kind rice at local market prices from the consumption module and using self-reported voucher value in local currency, with an imputation rule when the currency value is missing but item-level spending is reported.
observations.locator: Section II.A Fidelity to Program Design

observations.statement: A pre-period proxy-means-test percentile score, not used as a discontinuity running variable, is used to split the sample into a targeted-eligible group and a non-targeted group, with narrower cutoffs used for heterogeneity by poverty depth.

For continuous outcome variables, the paper states a uniform outlier rule of dropping any observation more than twelve standard deviations from the mean, applied consistently across the subsidy, consumption and price tables.
The rice-quality variable is constructed from a three-point Likert survey item and standardized onto a zero-to-one percentile scale before being used as a regression outcome.

As an alternative construction, the subsidy and consumption measures are recomputed by valuing quantities received at a common fixed set of local prices for both arms, so that the main results can be shown not to be driven by differential price valuation.
observations.locator: Section II.E Impacts on Poverty; Section III.B Prices

observations.statement: Regression tables report a row indicating stratum fixed effects are included, a row indicating double-lasso-selected controls are included, observation counts, the control-group mean of the dependent variable, and standard errors in parentheses with clustering and randomization-inference details in the table notes.

Rather than progressively adding control variables across columns, the main tables hold a single fixed specification constant and instead vary the estimation sample across columns by baseline poverty-score subgroup.

A single baseline specification (equation 1) is used throughout the main tables, with control variables chosen by an automated double-lasso procedure rather than a manually specified set, described once in the estimation section and then referenced in every subsequent table's notes.
Standard errors are clustered at the district level, and the paper justifies this choice explicitly as matching the level at which the program was randomized.

In addition to cluster-robust standard errors, the paper reports randomization-inference p-values from a fixed number of permutations of the treatment assignment in every regression table, citing prior methodological work on the fragility of asymptotic inference in this class of design.
observations.quote: we report randomization inference ­p-values in all tables

observations.statement: Although the design has a moderate number of clusters, the paper does not frame its parallel reporting of randomization-inference p-values as a response to a small-cluster problem; this appears to be an implicit rather than explicitly labeled few-clusters safeguard.

A baseline balance check across per capita consumption, caloric intake and asset variables is discussed in the main text with a joint F-test randomization-inference p-value, while the underlying balance table itself is placed in the online appendix.

A placebo-style check on local political outcomes, such as protests or turnover of village leadership, is reported in an online appendix table and summarized in a footnote as showing no observable treatment-related differences.

The paper reports a compliance diagnostic showing that assignment to the 2018 versus 2019 conversion wave was followed almost exactly, with only a small number of control districts converting ahead of schedule.
observations.locator: Section I.C Randomization Process and Compliance

observations.statement: A nonparametric figure of price effects against distance to the district capital is estimated with locally weighted regressions using a stated kernel type and bandwidth, functioning as a visual sensitivity check on the linear heterogeneity specification reported in the accompanying table.

The paper does not describe household-level survey attrition or nonresponse as a design concern, consistent with its repeated cross-sectional (rather than panel) survey structure; this is treated as not applicable rather than analyzed.

A footnote summarizes several robustness checks placed in the online appendix: dropping the lasso-selected controls, dropping the budget-driven holdout stratum, winsorizing the subsidy outcome, and splitting results by randomized conversion wave, stating that all give qualitatively similar results.

Poverty results are reported to be robust to alternative welfare metrics, including log consumption and constant-relative-risk-aversion utility under two risk-aversion parameters, with the supporting table placed in the online appendix.
observations.locator: Section II.E Impacts on Poverty, footnote

observations.statement: The paper reports that recomputing consumption and poverty using a common fixed price for rice and eggs across both arms yields results that are described as virtually identical to the main fixed-price-free estimates.

A footnote reports that repeating the main analysis using an earlier, smaller survey wave alone, or pooling both waves, produces similar results, despite acknowledging that the earlier wave has less statistical power because fewer treatment districts had converted by that date.

Heterogeneity by baseline poverty score is implemented as a series of progressively narrower prespecified subgroup cutoffs rather than as an exploratory post hoc search, with the primary two-way split stated to follow the pre-analysis plan.

Heterogeneity in price effects is estimated through interaction terms with several remoteness and supply-shock measures, explicitly motivated by price-theoretic predictions about where markets should respond more to a change in subsidized supply.

The administrative-fidelity mechanism is supported by a simple Nash-bargaining model in which the indivisibility of a debit card and a non-sunk negotiation cost for local officials under the new default jointly predict a point mass of beneficiaries receiving the full entitlement.

Evidence on which type of actor distributes benefits under each program is drawn from a purpose-run phone survey of district governments, used to substantiate the claim that distribution shifted from government officials to private bank agents.

Alternative price-theoretic channels, namely consumption flexibility, price effects and self-selection through food quality, are each tested and then characterized qualitatively as small relative to the main administrative-fidelity channel, without formally decomposing total effects into channel-specific shares.
observations.locator: Section III Alternative Mechanisms; Section V Conclusion

observations.statement: Throughout the results sections, treatment coefficients are interpreted as a percent change relative to the control-group mean of the dependent variable reported in the same table, rather than in raw units alone.

A back-of-envelope calculation converts the estimated quality-rating improvement into standard-deviation units of the local rice-price distribution to express the quality gain in an implied monetary price equivalent.
observations.locator: Section II.D Quality and Targeting, footnote

observations.statement: Administrative costs of the two programs are compared using a cost-as-share-of-benefits-disbursed metric, with a further scenario recomputing the voucher-side ratio under an alternative assumption about which agents' equipment costs are attributable to the program.
observations.locator: Section IV Leakage and Administrative Program Costs

observations.statement: The authors state a data limitation that the targeting lists used for analysis are not the exact final lists used by local governments for actual distribution, so some measured non-receipt among low-score households may reflect later list revisions rather than true exclusion error.

The paper explicitly caveats its price-heterogeneity analysis by noting it relies only on cross-sectional variation in local prices, which could reflect underlying local demand differences rather than a pure supply response to the program.

The conclusion caveats that the amount of aid reallocation found here depends on the accuracy of the government's underlying targeting data and on how communities use discretion when it is available, rather than being a fixed feature of switching to vouchers in general.

Nonparametric bin-scatter figures, with markers scaled by the number of households in each bin, are used as the main visual complement to each corresponding regression table across the results sections.

Every regression table's notes state the underlying data sources, the fixed-effects and control-selection rows, the standard-error clustering level, and the number of randomization-inference permutations used, applied as a consistent template across tables.

Online appendix tables and figures are numbered sequentially without a distinct alphabetic prefix and are referenced pervasively from main-text footnotes rather than reproduced, so many reported robustness and diagnostic results are only accessible outside the main PDF.
Regression tables report point estimates, clustered standard errors in parentheses and randomization-inference p-values in brackets, but do not mark coefficients with conventional significance stars.
Quantitative headline findings on assistance received and poverty reduction are previewed in both the abstract and the introduction, ahead of any description of the empirical design or data.
The introduction closes with an explicit roadmap paragraph naming each subsequent numbered section and its topic.
observations.quote: The rest of the paper proceeds as follows

observations.statement: Administrative and price-theoretic mechanism analysis is placed in sections after the main delivery, targeting and poverty results, and robustness checks are not collected into a single dedicated section but are instead folded into footnotes throughout the results sections, with supporting tables placed in the online appendix.
A paragraph early in the introduction states what data and randomized design let the study contribute relative to prior price-theoretic work comparing in-kind and voucher transfers.

The reference list cites a formal replication data package for the paper, deposited with the American Economic Association's data and code repository, distinct from the underlying restricted survey and administrative data.

Access to the administrative targeting database and its linkage to the survey is described as arranged through government partnership and analyzed only in de-identified form, distinguishing restricted administrative access from the publicly deposited replication package.

The trial is stated to be registered in a public RCT registry with a named trial identifier, and the main regression specification and the primary poverty-score subgroup split are stated to follow a pre-analysis plan.
observations.quote: registered in the American Economic Association Registry for randomized control trials

observations.statement: Institutional review board approval is stated in the author note, naming the reviewing institution and a specific protocol number.

The conclusion explicitly scopes the paper's administrative-fidelity explanation to settings of limited state administrative capacity, rather than presenting the finding as a universal ranking of vouchers over in-kind transfers.

gaps: No explicit statement on whether survey or sampling weights are applied in the main regressions.
No explicit discussion of the small number of clusters (105 districts) as a few-clusters inference concern beyond citing randomization inference and Young (2019) generally.
No explicit multiple-testing correction is described despite many outcome variables and nested PMT subgroups being tested across tables.

The online appendix, including the populated pre-analysis plan and most robustness and diagnostic tables, is not part of the provided text and could not be read directly; what it contains is known only from main-text and footnote descriptions.

reading.note: Read the full extracted text page by page: front matter, introduction, all of Section I (setting, sample, randomization, data, validity, estimation), Section II (delivery, targeting, poverty), Section III (mechanisms), Section IV (leakage and costs), the conclusion, and the reference list. The paper's online appendix is a separate document not included in this 34-page PDF/text extract and was not read; its contents are known only through the main text's descriptions and footnote pointers.
